text: DOCUMENT STATUS: SYNTHETIC / DEMONSTRATION ONLY This is a fictional policy written for the AeroSync portfolio project. It is not sourced from, and must not be presented as, an actual airline operations control manual. TITLE: AeroSync Aircraft Swap Policy (Demo) DOCUMENT ID: AS-SWAP-001
Defines when the resolution engine may propose swapping the aircraft assigned to a flight, and what conditions a proposed swap must satisfy before it can be presented for approval.

chunk_id: aircraft_swap_policy::When a Swap Should Be Considered::0
section: When a Swap Should Be Considered
text: An aircraft swap should be proposed when: - The originally assigned aircraft has a projected delay exceeding 90 minutes due to an unresolved technical or rotation issue. - A technical fault has been logged against the assigned aircraft that is not expected to clear before the flight's revised departure window. - Swapping unlocks a materially shorter cascade — i.e. the freed-up aircraft can recover a later flight's schedule by more time than the swap itself costs.

A candidate aircraft may only be swapped onto a flight if ALL of the following hold: 1. Same or greater seating capacity as originally scheduled, unless the load factor for the affected flight is below 70%, in which case a smaller aircraft may be used with duty-manager approval. 2. Valid maintenance status with no open deferred items that restrict the route or sector length in question. 3. The candidate aircraft's own schedule allows it to be released without creating a new disruption of equal or greater severity elsewhere in the network. 4. Crew already assigned hold a valid type rating for the candidate aircraft, or replacement crew with the correct rating are available within the delay tolerance.

Every proposed swap must include an estimated "cascade cost" — the total passenger-minutes of delay it is expected to introduce elsewhere in the network, weighed against the passenger-minutes of delay it prevents on the original flight. A swap should not be proposed if its cascade cost exceeds the delay it avoids.

Swaps that keep the aircraft within the same fleet type and route family may be proposed for standard approval. Cross-fleet swaps (e.g. narrow-body for wide-body) always require duty-manager sign-off regardless of projected benefit, due to the downstream crew and gate implications.
Every swap proposal must record: original aircraft, candidate aircraft, trigger reason, estimated cascade cost avoided, estimated cascade cost introduced, and approval status.

DOCUMENT STATUS: SYNTHETIC / DEMONSTRATION ONLY This is a fictional policy written for the AeroSync portfolio project. It is not sourced from, and must not be presented as, an actual DGCA regulation, airline manual, or any other official document. TITLE: AeroSync Crew Operations Policy (Demo) DOCUMENT ID: AS-CREW-001
This policy defines how AeroSync's resolution engine and duty officers should treat crew duty time, rest requirements, and reassignment decisions when resolving a flight disruption.

A cockpit or cabin crew member's duty period begins at report time and ends 30 minutes after the final flight of the day blocks in. Standard duty limits used by AeroSync's scheduling logic are: - Maximum single duty period: 13 hours for a two-pilot crew on narrow-body aircraft, reduced to 11 hours for duty periods with more than 4 sectors. - Minimum rest between duty periods: 12 hours, or the length of the preceding duty period, whichever is greater. - A crew member already at or beyond 10 duty hours is flagged internally as "high fatigue risk" and should not be assigned an additional sector without supervisor override.

Crew may be reassigned to cover a disrupted flight only if all of the following hold: 1. The reassignment does not push the crew member's projected duty period past the applicable limit in the section above, including the estimated duty time of the new sector. 2. The crew member holds a valid type rating for the aircraft in question. 3. At least 45 minutes of turnaround buffer remains between the crew member's prior sector and the new report time. 4. If the crew member's remaining duty margin before reassignment is under 90 minutes, reassignment requires duty-manager sign-off rather than automatic approval. Crew that are already within 60 minutes of their duty limit should not be reassigned under any circumstances; a fresh crew or standby crew must be sourced instead, even if this introduces additional delay.

Each base maintains a standby crew pool. Standby crew should be activated in preference to reassigning an already-flying crew member whenever the projected delay to activate standby is less than the delay that would result from waiting for the original crew to become legal again.

Every reassignment decision, whether automatic or manager-approved, must be logged with: crew ID, original assignment, new assignment, duty hours at time of decision, and the rule under this policy that justified the decision.

DOCUMENT STATUS: SYNTHETIC / DEMONSTRATION ONLY This is a fictional standard operating procedure written for the AeroSync portfolio project. It is not sourced from, and must not be presented as, an actual airline or regulatory SOP. TITLE: AeroSync Disruption Response SOP (Demo) DOCUMENT ID: AS-SOP-001
Defines the standard sequence of steps AeroSync's resolution engine and duty officers follow when a disruption is first detected, from detection through to logged resolution.

On detecting a delay, cancellation, or technical event, the system classifies its severity: - Minor: projected delay under 30 minutes, no downstream cascade risk flagged. - Moderate: projected delay 30–120 minutes, or a cascade risk flagged against fewer than 3 downstream flights. - Severe: projected delay over 120 minutes, cancellation, or a cascade risk flagged against 3 or more downstream flights.

For Moderate and Severe events, the resolution engine runs a cascade assessment across the affected aircraft's remaining rotation and any crew or gate dependencies, per the cascade simulation logic, before any resolution options are generated.

The resolution engine proposes resolution options drawn from the applicable policies: crew reassignment (see AS-CREW-001), gate reassignment (see AS-GATE-001), aircraft swap (see AS-SWAP-001), and passenger rebooking (see AS-REBOOK-001), ranked by estimated total passenger-minutes of delay avoided.

All Severe-classified events, and any Moderate event where the top-ranked option requires duty-manager sign-off under its own policy, are queued for human review before any action is taken. Minor events may be auto-resolved if the top-ranked option requires no sign-off under any applicable policy.

Once approved (automatically or by a duty officer), the resolution engine executes the selected option and writes an audit record containing: the triggering event, severity classification, all options considered, the option selected, who approved it (system or named duty officer), and the outcome.

Severe events are queued for post-event review within 24 hours, to check whether the cascade assessment's projected impact matched the actual outcome. Significant mismatches should be flagged for policy or model review rather than treated as one-off anomalies.

Any event where no resolution option can be generated that avoids breaching a hard limit in the referenced policies (duty time, minimum turnaround, swap eligibility) must be escalated to a duty manager immediately rather than left unresolved in the queue.

DOCUMENT STATUS: SYNTHETIC / DEMONSTRATION ONLY This is a fictional policy written for the AeroSync portfolio project. It is not sourced from, and must not be presented as, an actual airport authority regulation or official gate-management manual. TITLE: AeroSync Gate Operations Policy (Demo) DOCUMENT ID: AS-GATE-001
Defines how gates are assigned, reassigned, and prioritized when a disruption requires the resolution engine to reallocate limited gate capacity across affected flights.

When more than one flight is competing for a gate reassignment, priority is given in this order: 1. Flights already delayed more than 45 minutes. 2. Flights carrying passengers with tight connections (under 60 minutes to next departure) to more than 20 passengers. 3. Wide-body aircraft, which have fewer compatible gates available. 4. All other flights, prioritized by scheduled departure time.

Gate scoring should treat the following as minimum safe turnaround windows; a proposed reassignment that leaves less than this buffer should be flagged as high-risk rather than auto-approved: - Narrow-body (A320/B737 family): 35 minutes - A321 / stretched narrow-body: 40 minutes - Regional turboprop (ATR72 and similar): 25 minutes - Wide-body (B777 and similar): 60 minutes

A flight's gate should be reassigned when any of the following occur: - The incoming aircraft is delayed such that the current gate's minimum turnaround window (above) can no longer be met. - A higher-priority flight (per the priority order above) requires the same gate within the conflict window. - The assigned gate is not compatible with the aircraft type inbound (e.g. a wide-body aircraft assigned a narrow-body-only gate).

If no contact gate can be found within the delay tolerance for a flight, the flight should be assigned to a remote stand with bus transfer rather than held indefinitely for a gate. This should be treated as a last resort, since it adds passenger transfer time.
Every gate reassignment must be logged with: flight ID, original gate, new gate, aircraft type, trigger reason, and the resulting turnaround buffer under the new assignment.

TITLE: AeroSync Passenger Rebooking Policy (Demo) DOCUMENT ID: AS-REBOOK-001
Defines how passengers on a disrupted flight are prioritized for rebooking, and the thresholds that trigger automatic versus manual rebooking.

When rebooking passengers from a cancelled or severely delayed flight (delay exceeding 180 minutes), priority is given in this order: 1. Passengers with a documented medical or accessibility need. 2. Passengers who will miss a connecting international flight. 3. Passengers who will miss a connecting domestic flight. 4. Unaccompanied minors. 5. All other passengers, in order of original booking class (highest fare class first), then check-in time.

A passenger may be automatically rebooked onto an alternative flight without agent review if all of the following hold: - The alternative flight departs within 4 hours of the original scheduled departure. - The alternative flight has available capacity in the same or higher booking class. - The passenger has no special service request on file. If any of these conditions fail, the passenger should be queued for manual agent review rather than auto-rebooked.

These thresholds govern which passengers are flagged for compensation review (final compensation decisions are outside the scope of this policy and this system): - Delay of 2–4 hours: flagged for meal voucher eligibility. - Delay over 4 hours or overnight: flagged for meal and accommodation eligibility. - Cancellation with less than 24 hours' notice: flagged for compensation review regardless of delay length of the replacement flight.

Passengers traveling together under a linked booking reference should be rebooked onto the same alternative flight whenever capacity allows, even if this means a later departure than the earliest individually available option.
Every rebooking action must be logged with: passenger reference, original flight, new flight, priority tier applied, and whether the rebooking was automatic or manually reviewed.
